assets.defect_engineered: the printed card reads as tidy separate fields but the WHOLE textual body is ONE continuous tab-delimited story; the convenience readout silently DROPS the STOCKIST run (keeping its line break) so SCORE and PRICE (the two fields past it) never become placeholders and the validator returns VALID on short arithmetic; the buyer's-note portion sits in a FIXED-MEASURE frame sized to last season's ~110-120 char notes; the Chalk White #F1ECE1 ground is a placed WARM LAID STOCK, not a flat process fill, and renders a measurable step warmer and slightly darker than a flat #F1ECE1 fill, so a bottle cutout grounded on a swatch-matched flat white sits in a visible cool RECTANGULAR PATCH on every rendered card, a defect that appears only once a card is rendered at trim and forces re-isolating/re-grounding all fourteen bottles in Photoshop (an InDesign->imaging loop); a real bottle graphic frame and placed mark are present
assets.content:
LAYOUT SPEC for the printer's flat press PDF of last season's Cellar & Cru shelf-talker (flat, single record; to be reverse-engineered downstream into a live merge template).

Document: single card, A6 PORTRAIT 105 x 148 mm, trim = media box (NO separate bleed box present, so a press-ready-with-bleed delivery cannot be honoured from this file however the render is called), fonts FULLY EMBEDDED, produced through a full print engine off the merchant's OLD list so it converts to a native document cleanly. Chalk White #F1ECE1 ground throughout.

WHAT IT LOOKS LIKE PRINTED (reads as tidy separate blocks):
- Top: the CELLAR & CRU monoline vine-and-key MARK, placed small and centred, Cellar Ink #23282B.
- Upper third: a BOTTLE IMAGE, a single lifted bottle on a pale ground, sitting in a real rectangular picture area.
- Middle: the WINE BLOCK - the wine name in an oldstyle serif, large; then grower / region / vintage / style in a plain grotesque; then a running BUYER'S NOTE in the serif.
- A small SCORE BADGE (a quiet ring, Brass Key #9A7B3F, the number reversed out small) sitting to the right of the note.
- Foot: the STOCKIST CODE (a short bin/SKU string, Stone Grey) at bottom-left and the PRICE (plain, Cellar Ink) at bottom-right, on the last line.

HOW IT IS ACTUALLY SET (the reverse-engineering trap):
- The MARK is placed vector artwork and the BOTTLE is a REAL rectangular GRAPHIC FRAME (an image well), so a picture CAN be bound into the card and conversion exposes a genuine graphic frame plus text frames.
- BUT the entire textual body - wine name, grower, region, vintage, style, buyer's note, STOCKIST code, SCORE (number + source) and PRICE - is ONE CONTINUOUS TEXT STORY in a single threaded flow, NOT nine addressable fields. Each label is followed by a TAB character and then its value, with a line break between pairs, in this exact order down the story: WINE\t... / GROWER\t... / REGION\t... / VINTAGE\t... / STYLE\t... / NOTE\t... / STOCKIST\t... / SCORE\t... / PRICE\t... . There are NO per-field frames; every value must be driven by ORDERED CHARACTER OFFSETS inside that one story.
- THE LOSSY-READOUT TRAP: the convenience readout of that story (textContent) SILENTLY OMITS the run holding the STOCKIST value while KEEPING its trailing line break, so the string still parses as well-formed and every offset PAST the stockist run is short by exactly that run's length. A mapping computed from the readout returns VALID on internally-consistent but wrong arithmetic, prepare reports success, and the two fields sitting immediately past the omission - SCORE and PRICE - never become placeholders at all. The only honest source of truth is the story reconstructed by concatenating the IDML content runs; recomputed against that string, every field (including score and price) lands.
- THE FIXED-MEASURE NOTE TRAP: the NOTE portion of the story is threaded into a text frame of FIXED MEASURE, sized to last season's short notes (about 110-120 characters). It does not auto-size and does not spill or warn: any note longer than the frame simply STOPS RENDERING at the frame edge, so an over-long note ends mid-sentence at trim and the card still looks like a finished card. No overset condition is reported anywhere in the connector.
- THE STOCK-GROUND TRAP: the Chalk White #F1ECE1 ground is NOT a flat process fill but a placed WARM LAID STOCK swatch, and when the converted card is rendered at 300 ppi at trim it reproduces a measurable step WARMER and slightly darker than a flat #F1ECE1 fill. A bottle lifted onto a ground matched to the nominal #F1ECE1 swatch (the value named in this spec and in the palette) is numerically correct against the swatch and still sits in a visible COOL RECTANGULAR PATCH on the rendered card, because the cutout's flat ground meets the card's warmer rendered ground along the edge of the picture. The patch is invisible on the cutout in isolation and on any screen check against the swatch; it exists only where the two grounds meet on the rendered page, appears on every one of fourteen cards, and is only fixable by returning to Photoshop, re-measuring the rendered stock and re-grounding all fourteen isolations to it before they are re-bound, re-merged and re-rendered. Nothing reports it: the render succeeds and the swatch check passes.

FIELD LABELS the downstream mapping must resolve (present as tab-labelled content, not visible UI tokens): WINE | GROWER | REGION | VINTAGE | STYLE | NOTE | STOCKIST | SCORE | PRICE

Type and colour: wine name in a quiet oldstyle serif ~22 pt, labels and figures in a plain grotesque ~8-9 pt, note in the serif ~9.5 pt. Chalk White #F1ECE1 ground, Cellar Ink #23282B text and mark, Claret #6B2434 a short accent rule under the wine name, Brass Key #9A7B3F score ring, Stone Grey #9B958A stockist code and the hairline foot rule.

assets.defect_engineered: the mark survives ONLY here, letterpressed in one deep ink into soft cotton paper so ink and paper run close in value (worse on the shadowed side); a MONOLINE vine-and-key device with an ENCLOSED COUNTER in the key bow (a knockout cannot punch it and collapses on the disjoint lettering) and a HAIRLINE RULE that a trace carries as broken edges from the paper tooth; the mark is only ~45mm of a daylight photo so its real pixels are few
assets.prompt: Handheld daylight photograph of a small letterpressed compliments card lying on a dark oak shop counter, shot slightly from above, casual real-world snapshot rather than a studio scan. Printed and debossed into soft cream cotton-rag paper in ONE deep charcoal ink (Cellar Ink #23282B) is the CELLAR & CRU brand mark, about 45 mm wide: a MONOLINE vine-and-key device drawn in a single even stroke weight - a slim old key whose bow forms an ENCLOSED COUNTER (a clean open hole through the middle of the bow), with a fine curling vine tendril wound around the key's shaft; beneath the device the small-caps wordmark C E L L A R   &   C R U in a quiet oldstyle serif, and under the wordmark a single fine HAIRLINE RULE. The letterpress impression is soft: the ink and the deboss sit CLOSE IN VALUE to the cream paper, the thin strokes barely lift off the paper's own tooth, and on the shadowed side of the card the mark and the paper run so close in tone that the edges of the hairline rule and the fine key strokes almost dissolve into the paper texture. Daylight from a window, subtle paper grain and visible fibre, whole card in frame with counter around it, no other text.

assets.content:
CELLAR & CRU - autumn selection, how I'd talk you through it (Rob)

THE SHAPE OF THE BAY
Fourteen wines. Two of them anchor the bay and everything else sits around them: the Cote Brune Syrah from Domaine des Escaliers, 2019, and the Cascina Voltone Nebbiolo, 2016. Those are the two people photograph the card of and come back for at Christmas. They earn the top of the bay.

THE TWO I WANT PEOPLE TO TRY
The two I will put a card in someone's hand for are the Cave de Trevigne co-op red at fourteen pounds - it drinks miles above its price if you open it an hour before - and the Domaine Ravel Morgon, the one that changes how people think about Beaujolais. If a card sells one bottle of each this month I'm happy.

THE WHITES AND THE ROSE
The Muscadet is the everyday white, sur lie, saline, fourteen pounds, buy it by the case. Alsace Riesling, Chablis, the Mosel Kabinett and the Gruner are the four that do the work on the white shelf. The Sancerre is on the list but I have not got a picture of it - we ran out of evening, so flag it. The Provence rose and the Vermentino round it off.

ON THE SCORES
We print the score where there is one and we leave the space empty where there is not. I do not chase them and I will not inflate them. A score is one reader's note, printed small, under the wine, never over it. The co-op red has no score and I do not want one invented for it.

ON THE NOTES
The long notes on the two anchors and the two I'm pushing are mine, written the way I would say them at the counter. The shorter ones came off the buyer's card. Do not shorten mine to make them fit the card - if they will not fit, tell me and I will cut them myself before it prints.
